ca_lower_middle_earth.blurb: Lower Middle Earth is the rock outcrop that meets the loop trail at the south end of the Mission Gorge climbing zone in San Diego's Mission Trails park, close to the entry of a narrow corridor of short routes. About twenty-one lines mix trad, sport and top-rope, mostly on granodiorite. Grades run from easy 5.6 and 5.7 climbs through a solid middle of 5.8 and 5.9 to a handful of 5.10s and 5.11s, so a mixed party can all find something. The climbs are short, the rock is smooth and can feel stiff for the number, and nearby walls can hold shade. Cool mornings and the shoulder seasons suit it well.
ca_lower_middle_earth.parking_note: Leave the car in the dirt lots near the park visitor center off Father Junipero Serra Trail, then walk the loop trail south to reach the base.

ca_sunnyside_bench.blurb: Sunnyside Bench is a granite cliff on the north side of Yosemite Valley, a short stroll east of the base of Lower Yosemite Fall. It holds about twenty routes, almost all trad, with a lone bolted line. The grade spread starts at an easy 5.5 and builds through 5.9 to a cluster of 5.10 and 5.11 cracks, so it works for beginners wanting a first multipitch as well as for crack climbers after something harder. Expect a mix of good cracks and face moves, some polished rock on the popular lines, and long waits at the base on busy days.
ca_sunnyside_bench.approach: Walk the Lower Yosemite Fall trail to the bridge, cross it, and continue a short way east. A climbers' path leaves the trail and a brief scramble gets you to the foot of the cliff.

ca_dairy_queen_wall_left_side.blurb: The left side of Dairy Queen Wall sits in the Lost Horse area of Joshua Tree National Park, a short way from the Hemingway Buttress lot. Around twenty routes are mostly trad, with a couple of bolted lines and a pair of top-ropes. Grades range from scrambling terrain up to the low 5.11s, with most climbs between 5.7 and 5.10. The stone here is smoother and greyer than on the right side, with an occasional knob, and the cracks are less pronounced. Expect some scrambling to get to the base. It makes a good change of pace if the busier Hemingway walls are crowded.
ca_dairy_queen_wall_left_side.parking_note: Use the big paved lot on Park Boulevard that serves Hemingway Buttress.
ca_dairy_queen_wall_left_side.approach: From the lot, take the signed trail toward Hemingway, then peel off left to the foot of the wall. Some easy scrambling is needed to arrive at the base.

ca_trailside.blurb: Trailside is a hillside section of the Limbo area in Mission Gorge, within San Diego's Mission Trails park, right where the main trail reaches the rock. Twenty routes mix sport, trad and top-rope, with many top-ropes visible from the path below. Most climbs are moderate, clustering around 5.7 with another group near 5.10, plus a few easier and harder outliers. The granodiorite is smooth and can feel stiff for its grade. Two obvious easy classics make it a sensible stop for newer climbers, and it stays popular with local parties.
ca_trailside.parking_note: Leave the car in the dirt lots near the park visitor center off Father Junipero Serra Trail, then follow the loop trail up to the hillside.

ca_5_camp_4_wall.blurb: Camp 4 Wall rises above the famous Camp 4 campground on the north side of Yosemite Valley. Twenty climbs are mostly trad crack lines on granodiorite, with a few aid routes. Most free routes fall between 5.8 and 5.10, with a couple at 5.11 and 5.12. Expect liebacks, hand and fist cracks, offwidths, and steeper face sections. The wall faces southeast, so it catches morning sun and suits the cooler seasons. Despite its location by the campground it rarely feels crowded, and the approach is a steep haul up a gully and boulder field with no real trail.

ca_first_cliff.blurb: First Cliff is the main wall of Patricia Bowl, a high alpine granite cirque in the Rock Creek area of the Eastern Sierra near Mammoth Lakes, at roughly 10,600 feet. Twenty routes are mostly trad crack climbs, with a few bolted sport lines. Grades start around 5.8 and are concentrated in the 5.10 to 5.12 range, so it suits strong, experienced leaders. Many lines are two pitches, with a less inspiring first pitch leading to the best climbing above. Splitter cracks and sound granite are the draw, and the thin air at this height is worth planning around.

_expect.name: Other Side of the River Wall

ca_other_side_of_the_river_wall.blurb: Other Side of the River Wall is a bouldering spot on the Highway 4 corridor in the Bear Valley area of the Sierra, across the river from the Stanislaus River campground at about 6,200 feet. It is the largest group of problems at the campground, with twenty on a long wall of granite. Most are slabby, with a few overhanging bits, and many are tall, so pads and a spotter matter. The grades are gentle: lots of V0 and easier, a handful of V2s, and only a few problems from V3 to V5. Some landings and lines still need tidying.
ca_other_side_of_the_river_wall.approach: From the campground, cross the bridge over the river and follow the bank downstream a couple of hundred feet to where the wall begins.

_skipped.ca_nautical_nightmares: no fetched page describes this crag itself, only its parent areas
